utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in and around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, the Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. For the Prosecution, Douglas Stringer, Alex Demirdjian, Case Manager Thomas Laugel, and legal intern, Kathryn Fox.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The witness may be brought in. Yes, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. We're calling Mr. Adnan Abd El Razek as our next witness. And if we didn't put it on the record last week, let me just thank the Trial Chamber for organising the additional sessions to ensure we can complete his testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Witness. Thank you for coming to The Hague to assist the Tribunal. I suppose you will testify in English? Is that right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, sir. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please tell us your name and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Adnan Tawfiq Abd El Razek. I was born on the 4th of June, 1940.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You are about to make the solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth. I need to point out to you that you expose yourself to the penalties of perjury should you give false or untruthful information to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: May I ask you to now read the solemn declaration aloud that the court usher will give to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Abd El Razek. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Abd El Razek.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Before I begin with some of my questions, allow me to give you a little guidance. Since we both speak the same language, we should make a pause between questions and answers, perhaps count to three mentally to make sure there's a pause, as we have interpreters translating for the accused and other people outside the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You have stated your name on -- on the record, may I ask you to provide the Trial Chamber with your nationality or ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: I was born to a Palestinian family prior to the creation of the state of Israel in what is so-called the mandated Palestine. We are -- my family is an Arab Muslim Palestinian family who luckily did not leave the country after its occupation by then the Israeli forces. We stayed in the state of Israel as Palestinian Arab minority and I -- our identity historically and realistically, we're Arab citizens of Israel.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can I ask you to give us a brief overview of your educational background?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: With pleasure, sir. At my age as a good remember back on the good days of being a student. Never mind my high school as it is not -- I started my academic studies undergraduate the Hebrew University in Jerusalem. My major was social work. I worked as probation officer for seven years after graduation. Then I moved back to the Hebrew University to have my graduate studies and I was teaching at the Hebrew University for seven years social work. And then I was teaching in Bethlehem University in West Bank and Al-Quds University in Jerusalem. Then I decided to go for my Ph.D. I went to University of Michigan at Ann Arbor. I have a double major, sociology and social work. I finished my Ph.D. on August 19 -- 1982. And then I went to work for the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Is it correct to say that as of -- it is October 1982, I believe, that you started to work for the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: 1st of October, I moved to New York. I assume my work at the Political Department. Then it was Political and General Assembly Department. I worked until my retirement on 1st of July, 2000. All the time I was in the Political Department, even when I was borrowed or sent or volunteered to go with UNPROFOR 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, let's get to that period of time, Dr. Abd El Razek. Is it correct that in April of 1992, you were assigned to go on a mission to the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Actually I was supposed to go on -- end of March that same year. We arrived to Belgrade on the 3rd of April, 1992, and then the whole contingency of civil affairs were very limited, very small. By the time I arrived to Belgrade - very nice city, by the way - something happened in the airport in Sarajevo. The plane of -- of then -- or the late President Alija Izetbegovic was stopped and kidnapped by local forces, and I would say that was the mark of the unrest, which is a mild expression, but the mark of upheaval in -- in Sarajevo. We could not -- I could not arrive to Sarajevo then because of the situation. I was appointed to be the political advisor, if you wish, to the civil police of UNPROFOR, and then most of our commanders, civil commanders, commander -- military commander, civil affairs were in Sarajevo. I was supposed to be stationed in Sarajevo. We could not reach Sarajevo. And then we stayed for a week in Belgrade, which gave me the pleasure of being in that city and chat with people from all walks to realise how harsh was then in Belgrade the economic situation and the -- the -- the financial crisis. We stayed in a hotel. I regret it, I did [indiscernible] five stars, I paid hardly 12 dollars per night. This period was very difficult for all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, if I could ask you to go back a little bit before you arrive in Belgrade. In -- in New York before you departed, what type of preparation or training, if any, was provided for the task that was ahead of you?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: I would want -- I would like to say something that maybe then the UN leadership would not like to hear. The entire mission was arranged in a hurry, and in short period of time, at least the civil affairs had to organise itself in few days or maybe maximum ten days and to start planning and going around for -- being stationed in -- initially we used Bosnia as the neutral, quote/unquote, neutral territory, to host the civil affairs and the sector commander and -- and the logistic was Banja Luka, actually, but the major chiefs of -- of operations were in Sarajevo. They sent contingency of civil police and military to tour the occupied then Croatian areas. In New York was nobody to brief us, but we were sent to read whatever the Security Council then discussed or decided upon. Of course, I -- I did go and read the -- the deliberation on the first resolution, it was the 721/91. This is the slash, this is mine because, you know, I saw the comments all over, they say 721 of the security, but this is the mark in Security Council, S3. Anyway, on the resolution of the cease-fires creating the PAs or the protecting areas, and later on the vision of Vance, Cyrus Vance, special envoy to share this project, if you may call it, or to the mission. We knew very few things. This small episode, my colleague, I went to -- then it was no Google. I went to the atlas, I went to the British encyclopedia and I had to draw by hand drawing the areas taken from the British encyclopedia and I had both Croatia and Bosnia and with the names that then the -- the encyclopedia mentioned. In the first day or first week I was later on in Sarajevo. On my desk, I had this map. I was visited by one of the major or high-ranking Presidency, call it, officer and he saw the maps and he was mad at me because this map was something to do with ethnicity and -- et cetera. So the -- our knowledge of the entire area was very poor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Before I move on with my next question. I see you have some notes in front of you, doctor. As I explained to you before, this is not really a memory test, so unless you really need to refresh your memory, I think that the Trial Chamber would prefer that you don't have notes in front of you while testifying. Unless you really need to refresh your memory, then could you ask for permission. But can I you to not have the notes in front of you. I understand that you -- with the dates and the numbers it is quite complicated bu --

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Yeah. I'm a disciplined person, I'll do. But remember, I'm not young anymore, and particularly with dates and names, Your Excellency, you have to forgive me if I sometimes need to refer to my written memory, not this. I'm not -- I'm closing this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: And I appreciate these procedures. I'm not intending to be otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And as I say, if you ever need to look at your notes, you could always ask for leave to do so.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now I understand you explained to us the type of preparation you had. You mentioned the Security Council resolutions and the reports. Were you familiar with them at the time?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: With the Vance Plan, I read it. I'm not sure that then I totally comprehended what happens, and there is a difference between reading about the vision of the plan with the areas, functions, and the real mental perception of yourself. And I did then understood the major -- sorry, major points of the plan. If you wish, I can explain it now, what I thought then the plan was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Perhaps you could explain to the Trial Chamber, before you left New York, what did you understand the mandate to be and your task when you arrived in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Even in -- in the Security Council, in that reports of the Security ... Council was clear, almost differences of task for the military and those for the civilians. While earlier -- excuse me, for going back, we just finished as UN our successful mission in Namibia, and Namibia was led by civilians, by civil leadership, Mr. Ahtisaari, became later on president of Finland. He was assisted by police contingency and some guards on this. The Security Council based on the deliberation and the reports from the field felt that this time the mission -- cannot be handed or handled by only civilians. This is why they appointed Mr. Satish Nambiar, Indian General, very respected general with great integrity, to be the chief commander of that mission. And Mr. Thornberry, Cedric Thornberry, British citizen, as the head of civil affairs, to be advisor or escorting, helping, being a mentor, political mentor to the -- the -- Mr. Nambiar, and this is what happened. And he was supposed to lead our work as civilians, and I was, of course, a civilian. He was too busy to re-establish the whole hierarchy for -- for -- for handling this crisis with this vast things in -- but then I had the -- the chance or the opportunity to be with her -- with him, sorry, in Belgrade, forcefully, and then we talked more details about our missions. In New York, there was still euphoria of the success of Namibia and really did not pay attention to the details of what really we are going to do. And I regret that we did not have better knowledge of -- of what is going to be in the coming few months or years.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, when -- when you arrived in Belgrade, as you just explained a moment ago, you had the opportunity to speak with Mr. Thornberry about the mandate. Could you the tell the Court what was mandate? What were you expected to do in the region.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: I can -- I can explain the package, but, of course, I'm -- I'm more -- was interesting in -- in our duty as civil affairs. But the package was clear and -- for us at least. There was Cyrus Vance Plan which after -- during the signature or signing of the cease-fire in -- in Croatia, was to, (a), to consolidate the cease-fire, to disarm those -- to design or designate PAs or protecting area. And those protecting areas, we are to demilitarise those protecting areas, and to see that there's -- that civilian safety, but major thing was also that, you know, we were instructed to focus on as civilians is the return of the refugees, let alone, of course, not -- not to let further exploitation and further deportation of people from those areas. As civil affairs assisted or assisting both ways of the military, we were supposed to go to those areas and to see to it that, (a), there is really -- civilians are not targeted and civilians are not chased, civilians are not harmed, and to work on the exchange of the refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. In relation to what you just told us, I'd like to you take a look at a document which is 65 ter 5140. And that is at tab 41 of our list. You will see it in a moment on the screen in front of you. If you have a hard time reading on the screen, please let us know and we'll try to adjust the screen.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: If you can just enlarge a little bit, the font. Can we -- oh, yeah. Can I -- I cannot do it here myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You cannot handle the document but you cab ask us to move it around. If we start with the top right-hand corner, so we can see the date on the document --

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes, it is 15 February 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: 1992, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Before coming to court today, did you have an opportunity to review this document?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. You see in the initial paragraph that there are references to several Security Council resolutions --

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: 74 -- 740, this is the UNPROFOR thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Right. Now we have a second section at the bottom which deals with the recent developments.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And if we go to the second page, it's moving now. Yes, if we can enlarge it a bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very generally, you will see that there's a narrative of exchanges between political leaders. What I want to you look at is the next page, page 3. Under section 2, which is called: "Implementation of the plan." Starting at paragraph 9.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now looking at paragraph 9, it talks about the plan has already been submitted on the 11th of December, 1991. And what I want you to look at now is item 10, paragraph 10. It talks here about: "First, I should like to draw attention to the provision in paragraph 9 of the plan that the exact boundaries of the United Nations Protected Areas will be decided by an advance party of the United Nations force, after consulting local leaders." Now, at the time as you were leaving or -- when you arrived Belgrade, were you familiar with the concept of United Nations protected areas?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Not border, but areas, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The areas, yes. What did you know about the areas? How many were there and where were they?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: The major one were three and then add the fourth one. It was Sector Sarajevo was Knin area. Sector East which is the one that I later assigned to, and Sector West, closer to Zagreb. Sector East was really along the Danube River. The top, up there is Beli Manastir. And down Sombor, Erdut, Dalj, go to Vukovar and down all area. We are more familiar with the region that is close to Osijek because this was our way for -- interfering with the parties in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: This is called Sector East. And initially was -- sector commander was a Belgian, I think that lieutenant-general, but not colonel, above colonel. Chief of Staff also was Belgian, was contingency of seven, eight people, soldier, not more. Civil affairs was located or assigned to Mr. Lubin, and there was a second man in that sector, supposed to be second man. And this is what happens when we went to that sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Can you look at the next paragraph, 11. It deals with -- well, I'll look at it here for you. Paragraph 15 --

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Sorry. I want to take your attention to the second sentence which starts with: "In discussion with parties concerned, it has" --

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: This is paragraph 11?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: 11, yes.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: In the second line you see at the end it starts with: "In discussions with the parties concerned ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Yeah, yeah, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. And then it follows here: "It has emerged that the most practicable way of dealing with the weapons of the Territorial Defence units and personnel based in the United Nations protected areas would be for them to be placed in secure storage under a two-lock system, with one lock being controlled by the United Nations force and the other by the president of the council of the opstina concerned." Now were you familiar with this concept of a two-lock system?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: We call it double locked. Call it double locked. I'm sorry, but this reminds me of some funny things happening in -- the arms were supposed to be double locked and supposed we have control on this. The time I was in Erdut was a short time. I seen men are -- armed vehicles running all over, they were not locked. I seen tanks. And then when I left, there were stories about how some people from ours handled those -- those double locks. I prefer not to mention that incidents but this is a bit painful. We did not really had at the beginning initially control. The JNA was stationed in -- in the boat, east of Dalj, but the boat was surrounded by big forest, hosting a clear military camp with heavy equipments, guarding not only the boat but, you know, being there around. They impose on us curfew and blackouts, and they moved through night-time. When we go to meet the general in the boat, we were escorted by their vehicles with no lights. And I was wondering how they could see the road, but -- but the JNA would say clearly that we are out of the areas. Yet you will see JNA contingency in the morning or day around -- around our place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And if I asked you to look at the next paragraph, which is 12, it says: "With reference to paragraph 11 of the plan, I have come to the conclusion that, for technical and practical reasons, it would be better for the force's headquarters to be located at Sarajevo, although the logistics battalion would be headquartered at Banja Luka." I think you made a reference to this at the beginning. Is this accurate?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes. Yeah, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. And paragraph 13 deals with the fact that the plan provides for a civilian chief for this mission. I believe you've looked at this paragraph which continues onto the -- the next page and which suggests, and if we go to the top of the next page. At the top of the next page you see the sentence which starts with: "I intend therefore to entrust the overall command of the United Nations operations to the Force Commander." Is that what happened on the ground?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: I just mentioned that at the beginning of my statement that while in Namibia was the -- the mission was run by civilian. In the former Yugoslavia, was run by general -- initially, or the first year, General Satish Nambiar as commander of the missions, while Cedric Thornberry was the -- assisting him in civil affairs. It is, you know, the -- the major surprise to our teams and to our mission, and you mention earlier how much we knew about -- about the region, is that we believed, and I don't know if it is naively, that Sarajevo would be safe and Banja Luka would be safe and our people were functioning from those places in a safe and organised way. It took very few weeks to realise that even Sarajevo was not safe for the mission to operate, and not Banja Luka, definitely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification, Dr. Abd El Razek.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I tender this document please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, document with 65 ter 05140 receives number Exhibit P2296.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Mr. Abd El Razek, you told us that when you arrived -- you arrived in Belgrade initially.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Before moving on to Erdut, how much time did you spend in Belgrade approximately?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: We arrived the 3rd of April. We left the morning of the 11th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And while you were in Belgrade, what kind of work did you do there?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: First of all, we definitely were following every morning the sitrep. Sitrep is the situation reports written by the military contingency. We call it "sitrep" shortly. And we were, of course, following the news all around, following the incidents in Sarajevo, wondering what will happen to our mission. And then, of course, during the day with Mr. Thornberry and I think there were three of us only, civilians and that is -- we'll try to figure out our mission what to do, what to do, et cetera. This seven or those seven days were a good break for me, because then I could re-educate myself on -- on -- on the -- on this issue, and to take a brief breath before I started. I was a little bit, of course, disappointed that I was not sent immediately to Sarajevo but then I was sent to Erdut.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: The -- the sitreps that you mentioned, where were they coming from, from which locations?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Still -- still was Sarajevo is the headquarter. We have small -- then small office [indiscernible] in Belgrade and smaller in Zagreb. But the sitreps will come from the commander's office. They normally are written and sent by the Chief of Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And then the sitreps themselves, which -- the information that was in the sitreps, which area did it cover?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: The Belgrade sitreps that we received mostly on the PAs areas. In Sarajevo, they came later because they themselves did not what was happening in Sarajevo. And most of the reports, the military reports, sitreps, came each sector with details of that morning, et cetera, what happens. Clashes, fighting, and mostly - mostly, unfortunately, sadly - how many people were deported or expelled in that -- that area. The civil police has its own report but they did not call it "sitrep" and they did not report on daily on a -- to -- to -- to the participants over there. And civil affairs, you know, being assigned, allocated, to work with them, they would send me a few things but very, very, very few. In the areas where -- the hot areas, and particularly then it was Knin, very hot area, UNMOs, United Nations Military Observers, were reporting, but not directly to us, to the headquarter and the headquarter would write the sitreps and send to headquarter New York to Mr. Goulding, who was then the undersecretary for peacekeeping --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: With respect to the sitrep that you reviewed while you were in Belgrade, what did you learn about the situation in the PAs, in the protected areas?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: I will be -- pretended that I knew everything then. No. I -- I -- the impression was (a) then -- I'm telling impression and forgive me if I don't go to the details because the whole thing is confusing. The impression was, (a), the cease-fire not always was maintained or kept. That from here and there, there are still fighting. That -- and mostly for our -- as civilians our civil contingency the ethnic cleansing, that's all then called ethnic cleansing, or the expelling of non-Serbs residents from those area continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, with respect to what you just told us I would like you to take a look at a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Which is 65 ter 5882 at tab 8. I have a note here saying that is under seal. Perhaps it shouldn't be broadcasted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: March 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. So this is before the time you were deployed, a week or so. When you arrived here in The Hague a few days ago, did you have an opportunity to review this press release?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, in the upper header we see "Republic of Croatia, Ministry of Information." As you say, 24th of March, 1992. And if we look at the first sentence here, it discusses that: "The Office of Interethnic Relations with the Croatian government sent today a letter to the command of UNPROFOR and the EC mission asking them to make efforts to prevent forced deportations of the non-Serb population from the occupied areas of Croatia." Now you mentioned this a moment ago --

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: -- is this the sort of information that was available to you while you were in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Not -- not -- not this. We have more -- more press reports on those, and not -- not the Croatian -- I was not made available, not exposed to any -- then any Croatian reports. I -- we -- we hardly had any reports from the fighting forces. We had mostly from our sources, and UNMO and the sector commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now with respect to the substance of this report, it continues on to talk about the escalation and deportations. It mentions here the ethnic groups that are concerned. Now, did you have this type of information available to you from the sources that you were reviewing?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes. From -- from UNMO and from, of course, the sitreps we talked about, but not at 23rd of March because I was not in the mission then.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: In Belgrade we had those reports on -- if you wish, I can tell you. The day we arrived -- on the 11th, actually, of April, we had full report on -- for deportation areas. Dalj was 110 if I remember. In Erdut, in Beli Manastir, and there is the city in the south, very south-east of the Croatian area. What's it called? And yesterday I had it in mind. It started with P. A city in -- in -- bordering the new south, very south-east of Sector East.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And let's get to Erdut. First of all, you mentioned now the 11th of April as a date that you arrived.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Where exactly in Erdut did you arrive to?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: The headquarter of UN in Erdut was the very north-east of the village. Apparently it was either an old camp or -- there are some ruins around it, Ottoman ruins or Turkish ruins. It was two buildings -- this is the very first -- the very last buildings on the villages. No -- not any building north of that area. If you go north and if you go to top of there -- of the building you see the river. It was a building, a small building that served the military and that sector commander, and small building that we civilians stayed is -- and dining room. I think that even the road from the main road was lasted there. Going to ours it was -- it was sand road, was not really a -- an organised or [indiscernible] road. This is -- we were -- the whole -- the whole village is not very big. Yes? I mean, you could walk from there to, whatever you call it, mid town. So that meant the village was walking distance. But we were stationed away from the building, from citizens -- from the citizens in that area. I cannot tell if it was really former military place or not. This -- I cannot recall that I knew this.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now upon your arrival in Erdut, who -- who do you find there at the barracks?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: We were immediately received by the sector commander and the civil affairs commander who was -- Mr. Zitterman was the chief of civil police, and Mr. -- and General Hoover -- Hoven -- was the sector commander and Jean Pierre is Chief of Staff. Were -- we hardly had a coffee and then Mr. -- or General Satish Nambiar arrived to give us briefing and to discuss with us our missions. I cannot tell, and I did not ask, whether it was co-ordinated that he will come to brief us or accidentally he came, but luckily he came and we could have chance to talk with him and to hear him and to clarify our mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, as part of the civilian affairs there, who was your direct supervisor?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: We were three people in that place. Jim Lubin, British citizen, who was UN official earlier and retired, and upon retirement he was joining that programme. And his wife, young wife. I regret I don't remember her name.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: He was supposed to be the -- a civilian officer of -- of that -- the sector. We call it chief of civilian co-ordinator of the sector. And myself, of course, and mostly we considered then that -- the civil police to be on our side, not on the military side. This is our colleagues because this -- mostly we talked about civilian things and was -- we felt okay. It was good -- good team. Not big team. Not -- not fantastic team, but it was okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And very briefly, Mr. Jim Lubin himself, who was he reporting to?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Our chief, it was, of course, Cedric Thornberry. We call it CT. And if you see that reports to him, we'll address as CT, Cedric Thornberry. He was then still stationed in Belgrade. And we sent our report to him. Bureaucratically and orderly and ranking speaking, he would sign the report, not me. Whether it is action that -- done by me or the civil affairs or the others, police affairs, Mr. Thornberry -- Mr. Lubin would be reporting directly to Mr. Thornberry.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now before we get into the details of your time in Erdut, can you tell us how much time did you spend in Erdut?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: I arrived on 11th, afternoon. I left on the 21st of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. And again, very briefly, where were you stationed to next?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: The coming few days, I was requested to go to Zagreb to brief the internal minister and the chief of police on the incidents that took place a day earlier in Marinci. I went with chief of civil police, was the name, a Norwegian officer, fine gentleman, Kjell Johansen, his name. We went to the internal minister to have an extreme attack on us and how there we helped the Serbs in the sector deporting 400 non-Serbs the day earlier from Ilidza. I was trying to explain. Luckily the blame went to Lubin not to me personally, and -- and this is -- we spent two days in Zagreb. Then I have to -- to be stationed back in Sarajevo, and you know then transportation, communication connecting to Sarajevo was not via the missile system, via the transportation today. We had to go to cross through Croatia, almost down to the shore, back to Sarajevo. Took us something like 14, 16 hours from the airport of Zagreb to reach Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Doctor, I don't mean to interrupt you but just, very briefly, how many time did you spend in Sarajevo, in total?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: All in all, if excluding the 11th, ten days.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Just for the record, Your Honours, the exhibit which was admitted, P2296, I'm informed that it should be admitted under seal. We just did a verification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. To be admitted under seal, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, returning back to Erdut, you told us that when you arrived you were received by Zitterman who was the civilian --

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Zitterman, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes. By that time had the UNPROFOR arrived in the area?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: UNPROFOR is -- is -- civil police is UNPROFOR, was part of UNPROFOR, but sector commander was sitting there. If you are talking about the massive deployment, no. We had sector commander, the Chief of Staff, and four, five assistant people sitting with him in that headquarter, military, and the three of us civil affairs, and two police -- civilian police in -- in this. And we had a civil police station in Dalj and we had UNMO along that border with Osijek. This all UNPROFOR. We are together, I believe, not -- fill normal bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that in Sector East there was a commander who was part of the Belgian contingent. How large was the Belgian contingent there?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Now, of course, later on, and gradually a Belgian battalion came to be stationed in Beli Manastir. Beli Manastir is over the bridge, overlooking -- it's something like, well, I would say, in normal drive, not crazy drive, something 40 minutes from Erdut through the main road. There was a Belgian battalion led by Colonel Joachim [phoen] I believe his name was. They were supposed to deal with mostly the area of Beli Manastir. I haven't seen them coming down to Erdut or to Dalj. They were not -- totally were not part of that. And then, a few days after I arrived, we had something like 20, 25 young Russian soldiers arriving to the headquarter to be under -- and I failed maybe to mention that the deputy sector commander was a Russian colonel. So, actually -- the way -- the way the forces were distributed or allocated or distributed is not something with the battle or war arrangement. Headquarters either at the sector or the chief headquarter will have representative of the battalions of -- of countries that were deployed their battalion under the flag of the UN, the UNPROFOR. So every headquarter, the people in that headquarter, the people in the sector would be representing the battalions. Some of them not but mostly yes. Definitely a sector commander will be represent the major power, major forces in that region. So in Erdut because of the presence of the -- of the Belgian battalion, so the Belgian commander was -- the commander was a Belgian commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Very well. Now, before getting into specific events, Dr. Abd El Razek, could you tell us, upon your arrival, what were your assignments, what were you expected to do as part of your role in the civilian affairs?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: To be honest with you, with the Court, of course, with Your Majesties, we were close to guessing what we would be doing next morning, but definitely in the sense of theoretical mission or political mission, we knew as civil affairs we had to take care of the civil affairs of the people in the PA areas, not the military affairs, not to interfere in, what they call it, the double lock, army, or the cease-fire, or chasing fighters around. UNMO was to register those violations. The civil police is to receive complaints of the civilians. The civilians would go to the civil police, but later on, when we arrived, civilians start coming to us, not to civil police. We were supposed to work with whatever we had, and then the Red Cross and UNHCR, United Nations High Commission for Refugees, and others to see, (a), if you can help the people of that -- that region with this crisis, stressful situation, and hopefully that, in time, will be facilitating the return of some of the refugees. To find out that immediately after we arrived, and I -- we -- we were briefed immediately when we arrived on three, four incidents of hundreds of deportees from PA from the area, including Erdut, that the 8th or 9th of -- of April, two days before arrive, were deported 110 or something from Erdut, something from area of the villages of Vukovar and Beli Manastir. I remember something, vaguely something like a total 400-something, 500 people were deported between the 7th and the 10th of -- of -- of that month and, of course, this is horrifying and we felt immediately that this is our project. We cannot let this go. And we start our communications. The first one was really -- that night, I think, or the night before the -- that night, I think, we went to meet the general, the boat general, the JNA, because the civil police has already the reports so we could -- we have material to go and to discuss it with him. And then we started looking for the civil authorities around to see if we can do something about this. So -- I would say we concentrate mostly on -- not, of course, not the return of the refugees but the prevention of further expelling people on this, with very, very limited ability and means and presence. Your Excellency, if -- we came to protect those people. We came to provide them with help. We were subjected to curfew and blackout, and we accepted this. I regret it. I regret it that UN accepted such a provision. While you have clear mandate by the Security Council, whether it's Chapter 6 or 7 does not make any difference because Chapter 6 -- plenty to do in this. We accepted. Why we accepted was too small potato to challenge this, but I was wondering why we accept. We are coming here to protect civilians and then we could not move in the evening, and most of the actions, most of the action were done after evening. If you permit me, may I have some water. I want to show you the pattern -- just to explain the pattern of this. In the evening, armed people will go to marked houses, marked not by -- by ink or something, but marked, those are non-Serbian houses. They start shooting at the windows, doors, in the air. They kill animals. I know that one evening that they kill two horses, and I mean, a guy was crying and I wish they killed my son not the horses. But this is something else. Horses. And then they leave. Then the police come in the morning. They call them, said, What happened to you? Police would say, Listen, those are military men. He will not say any milicija or some military, armed people, not from here, not ours, and we cannot help it but we advise you to leave, for your safety, please leave. Now some of them will get the hint, some others no. They call the next evening, do the same thing but escalated. And those people come to back the police to let them leave. This was repeated [indiscernible] not only Erdut, Osijek, Beli Manastir. I witnessed in Beli Manastir two families that I help leave that area. The same story. In the evening, boom boom boom boom. The doors, windows, animals, thieves, and the morning say, Hey, guys, the only choice you have is to leave. We cannot protect you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now let's go back on -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry, just before this is lost on the transcript and I fully understand why the word was used at -- at page 24, line 11, the Serbian word that was used there, but I believe that my learned friend and I will both agree that the word that was actually used by the witness based upon the word that he has used in his statements is not the Serbian word. It's in fact the English word. I don't want to use the word.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I will clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Just a second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Couple of tell matters, Your Honour, as ... Yes. First of all, with respect to the exhibit which was admitted and a moment ago I said it should have been under seal, I was incorrect. That one is to be kept public. It is the document which was on the screen, the press release that we have on the screen which was not to be broadcasted. I think we had said that earlier. So for the record, P2296 does not have to be under seal. And the document that we have on the screen right now was not to be broadcast, so if it was, we can redact or -- no, it was not. Okay. We can remove it from the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm not quite -- I'm not following. You say the press release should not be -- can be public.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And then the next one? Because I had still had a press release on my screen. Which one is the next one?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: So the press release that was on the screen, 65 ter 5882, was not supposed to be on the screen, whereas the United Nations report from April 1992 that we tendered, P2296, that one can be admitted in public. I made an error and I asked for it to be admitted under seal, so that one can remain in public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Is that clear to you, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I apologise because I'm properly injecting the confusion. The one mistake that does still exist is that the press release, tab 8, is 65 ter 5882. And at the moment the transcript incorrectly indicates that it was called up as 65 ter 5828. So it's not 5828. It's 5882. And that is at page 16, line 9, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And if we can still help it, it should not be broadcasted? Right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record, 5882 was not broadcast at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise, Dr. Abd El Razek. We'll return now to the portion of your evidence. You told us earlier that the first night you went to the JNA headquarter on the boat. First of all, were you aware of what was the name of the unit or where it came from?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: JNA is -- I'm sorry, but -- it's written somewhere. I cannot verify it right now but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Abd El Razek --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- just one moment, please. Mr. Demirdjian, are you now addressing Mr. Gosnell's problem with one word?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I will come to that as part of my examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I plan on doing that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sorry. I don't mean to be persnickety about this but I would suggest that it was a transcription error so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me deal with it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Earlier, Dr. Abd El Razek, you said the word "milicija," I believe. Can you tell us, how do you understand this and how do you spell it and -- yes.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: There's an army with uniforms that each army, national army would identify itself, as the civil police, police, I dealt with police all my life, I know -- whereas arms people who go around with same uniforms with fully machine-guns and weapons, with berets, one green and red in my area, we in general terms call them militia, not milicija, militia. If you wish, I can call them fighting arm -- armed people, armed persons, arm -- I'm -- I did not invent the term, milicija. We call them the militia. And it was the militias in Lebanon, the militias in this, militias in this. It's a very common term. If, Your Excellency, you want to use a different concept, I have no control of this. I am not the owner or the inventor of such a concept.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: No, I do see the problem, Your Honours. It's because the term militia was used once in the transcript with a t, whereas now it is being used with the Serbian, where it's milicija.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Abd El Razek, am I correct in assessing that you're referring to militia?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Militia, not milicija. And I didn't say Serbian milicija, I said militia. You know, I did not look at their IDs, I -- but it is -- it is to become known that those militias belonged to groups of Serbian fighters with the locals and mostly locals but not only locals. Some people came from Belgrade came to fight and others. I don't want to tell the story. I think it is known. If it is not known, I'm apologising to confuse. But those fighters were the main forces on the ground to perform the ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Abd El Razek, you probably know what in Serbian is referred to as militia, right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know militia is police --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- and it's not the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And this is not what you meant --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- when you used this word.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Are we --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't -- I don't name the police. We call it polica. Polica with c-a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Problem is solved.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I think the problem is solved, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Dr. Abd El Razek, with respect to the JNA unit which you saw on the boat, how many times did you go to the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: I believe three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And who did you meet with there?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Now we will go, first of all, Lubin and the chief, the commander of the -- the sector commander, the Belgians, myself, and meet. There was two personalities, two people, one is the high commander, the general, and one the assistant or the deputy. I think that one time we met with the deputy, twice we met the general. We also met the general later on. This is something else on the boat of Osijek, on the case of -- of that village. But on the boat we went three times.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And to be clear, how did you communicate with the local JNA commanders?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Our military commander would do that. I mean, the -- our Belgian -- they do. I -- I believe that --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I apologise, I meant with respect to language.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Oh. We had -- we have translator. We had a young guy from Beli Manastir with us, a [indiscernible] I don't remember now, but -- Your Excellency, you have to forgive me. This is 20 years old and the names is a bit -- a bit problematic but, you know, I can visual. 20 years from now I can describe this sitting but not names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: It isn't but natural, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We had an interpreter from this -- a nice guy and intelligent who would come with us for interpretation. The generals, nobody spoke English.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now with respect to the three times that you met the JNA generals or his deputy and your relations with the JNA, can you tell us what was your impression of the role of the JNA in the region?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: We were very frustrated, extremely frustrated because this is like ping-pong. Go to JNA, they tell us nothing. Go to police, it's not me, go to the -- later on we'll talk about Mr. Hadzic, no, not me. Nobody is admitting that the control and what's happening on the nights and the days on the streets of -- of the whole sector. But the JNA generals were stressing and they want us to send the message clear to our headquarter that JNA is out of the territories, that the boat is in the Danube, is not -- is outside the areas. Yet there is a camp surrounding that -- that boat. It is in Croatian traditional -- Croatian territory. And you see -- from time to time we saw tanks, armed vehicles, those are not police, except who come maybe to [indiscernible] police was starting using or were starting using PC armed vehicles, colour them with a police -- with the police marked colours. But the JNA was in on the ground, and they were denying total involvement on the complaints that we were presenting or conveying, and we could not use their authority to stop this mess of semi-military personnel going around doing the job, including humiliating us. We had from our headquarter north to Beli Manastir, down to Osijek, at least four check-points manned, not the police, not the army, but also I call them militias. No English, but pushing with a gun. This is something that the JNA will continue denying any -- any responsibility in the access. They also denying that they have any political influence in this. It's not -- they're out. We are clean, we're out.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you just mentioned a few topics here. What were the subjects of the conversations you had with the JNA commanders?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Details with complaints, bring complaints of people, of local people. We bring to them, brought to them UNMOs' reports, United Nations Military Observers, we bring to them the civil affairs reports on what's happening the night before or the week before or the two days before on this ethnic cleansing manufacture, ethnic cleansing project, ethnic cleansing activities. These are the main -- as civilians this is our main -- we did not discuss any military things with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, you told us earlier that there was a curfew that was in place.

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Were you aware of who was enforcing the curfew?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: When we arrive, and before that, our commanders would inform us of the curfew. The military commander, the sector commander, and then the civil police. And we never verified clearly who's enforcing this but that the civil police, the local civil police deny any -- any access or any control over this or anything to do with this. The local police, not our civil police. The local police that we talked with them about this, they deny any -- any -- any charge of these things. They later on they refer us to other people that responsible of what's happening to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, coming to that topic, who did they refer you to?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Just as introduction. When go to the police, they will tell you, Mr. Adnan, Mr. Lubin, this, we understand, and, by the way, I must say, and I say that also in Bosnia, many of them are very respectful people. They are educated, they have -- they know the law, they know what civil rights means, and many of them were embarrassed to see what was happening, especially the higher rank but some of them are associated -- they will tell us, Listen, we have no control on those people going around and shooting. But when we pushed them, later on, they refer us to Mr. Hadzic. Said, If you want to solve this problem, you have to go to Mr. Hadzic. He is the commander of this. He's the chief. We cannot argue with him. We cannot stop them. This is Mr. Hadzic's project. This is how and when we decided to go and meet with Mr. Hadzic. Based on -- on -- on the police, a denial of their responsibility, be hinting to us, not hinting, more than hinting to us that Mr. Hadzic is responsible for these things and we have to appear to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now you mentioned a moment ago that this was information that was provided to you through your contacts with the local police?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Local -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now, what was the -- how frequently were you in contact with the local police?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: The ten days I was there, I would say at least eight times we met with the police. I never went to any police station there. I know that there is police station down in Dalj but not in Erdut. We have them -- communicate with them, they come to our place. Sometimes we met them at the winery. But -- and those guys, persons, gentlemen, whatever, would say, Hey, we have no responsibility. I remember once that the guy with the two horses were shot. I went to the police and said, Listen, why horses? They don't have any -- anything to do. They said, Mr. Adnan, it's not -- we did not do that. We -- we -- nothing. I mean, we feel sorry. And horses from that region, meaning the farming region, horses and animals and cats -- cattles were the assets of their life. And the police knew that. So they will not -- they will say, It's not our responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: When you reported these complaints to the local police, what, if anything, did they do?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: I doubt if they did anything. I know that some of the local, future deportees then were afraid to go to the police too because they were telling us that the police would report them to the -- I don't know if you don't like the militia, I'm sorry, but this is the expression that we -- we discussed, that they will report them to the militia. So actually that -- the citizen -- they did not know even if they could trust us. They have nobody to trust around. They are left -- excuse me for the expression, with no God. And go and do something about it with curfew, blackout. Two soldiers and two civil police with no arms and yourself with nice necktie and [indiscernible].

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Now earlier you said that when you were speaking to the police they told you you have to go to Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: What did you do about that?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: We asked the police themselves, the local, to arrange for us a meeting with Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when did that happen?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: And happens, Mr. Lubin, his wife, myself, and the interpreter, we went and were escorted towards -- the police take us to this and then they handed us to the army personnel around. They took us to his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Where was this office?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: This area is a strange within this village that nowhere. There was a nice winery area. And within an area there is a castle and the hangars and there's a building. We went to the building, not the castle. I believe, if I'm wrong maybe [indiscernible] but I know that we were escorted through an opening or a door with an office to his office.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Can you -- can you describe the office. What did it look like?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Office was simple, not -- not fancy. A lot of key personnel that you have no privacy even sitting there and [indiscernible] and lots of communication that's come and how supposed to have this talk [indiscernible] and Mr. Hadzic was there. He was with darker beard. We're all getting old. And -- yes. He was -- the first time we went, we spent something like 45 minutes with him and we told him our story about what's happening in the night, in the day, on -- on -- on -- ethnic cleansing or -- and forced expelling people, forced deportation. And, of course, we discuss also matters of the UN, our headquarter, what is this, what is that, but mainly we went to complain and to ask his help to stop this ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Who was present during your meeting with Mr. Hadzic?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Beside Lubin, his wife and myself and interpreter, lot of people goes and comes, but I cannot recognise them. The police did not enter with us to that place.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: And when you say "a lot of people," what did they look like?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: The one that I describe as militia people with armed --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: How did the militia look like?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: It depends what area coming [indiscernible]. I don't want to be dealing with ethnicity and -- and -- be careful not to go to Lombroso description. Some of them, they look very bad, very sloppy, very -- with not really serious look and dress and this, but a lot of arms. Some of them were more sophisticated, looks more apparently, if I may, Your Excellency, say they don't look like peasants. And some of them looking very much as peasants.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: What kind of clothing did they have?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: Always close to khaki, but not really camouflage, there's no -- red and green. Mostly green in our area, I think [indiscernible] or something. Some of them with not beard, big one, but unshaven. I guess. Not beard. The one in -- in -- in -- I met down in that village was -- was beard. I -- I don't want to be somebody who classify people or claim or pretend they can, I can, identify identities of peoples by -- by -- by this -- but we were told the difference between the real Chetniks and -- in the militia, the new ones. I -- I cannot -- I cannot, but I saw earlier in -- in Belgrade people look like a Chetnik, like [indiscernible] that were fancy dressed, et cetera -- I don't know. I cannot tell what is the difference. I cannot be responsible of making any differentiation of bodies or nose or eyes or ears. I'm not Lombroso fan.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: That's fine, Dr. Abd El Razek. Before we break for the day, could you tell us what was Mr. Hadzic's response to your report?

utterances.speaker: ADNAN ABD EL RAZEK
utterances.text: It was strongly, very strong response on -- on -- on -- on denying, on saying, Not my people. How come you want to know about it? This with -- then brought us to understanding with him and then with the rest, that next time that people want to leave voluntarily, freely, they will, the police will come to us to verify, to make it clear that those people want to leave voluntarily, on their own, and not force, and this was not a written agreement, gentlemen agreement, verbal agreement. There's -- Mr. Hadzic pledged that his people -- and don't ask me if he defined his people. He did not define his people. His people will -- and the police will help us verify or help those people leave voluntarily not forced.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: I think it's the appropriate time for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Indeed, Mr. Demirdjian. Mr. Abd El Razek, this is the end of the today's hearing. We will see you again tomorrow morning at 9.00 for the morning hearing. You're not released as a witness, which implies that you -- which implies that you are not allowed to discuss with anyone your testimony, nor are you allowed to speak to any of the parties. You understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will not disappoint you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. The court usher will escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Have a nice evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] You too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, time-wise, and only time-wise --

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: -- is your examination-in-chief going as you wish it would go? If you understand what I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, I do issues. We're expecting to not take the entire four hours as we had initially announced, and I expect to finish within the first session tomorrow. Again depending on the answers, but I do understand, and, if necessary, will focus the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: That's good to hear, Mr. Demirdjian, that, if necessary, you will focus the witness. If there's nothing else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Demirdjian, the press release, is that to be tendered or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Oh, we didn't tender. Yes. Yes, please, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Oh. Then I shouldn't have asked the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry to have to do it. The source, it's a press release from the Ministry of Information of the Republic of Croatia. There are some very loaded allegations in this press release and some specific information that this witness could not confirm and the witness in fact said he had never seen this press release or any other press release because that wasn't where he was getting his information. So in relation to what the witness knew relative to what -- the specific information in the press release, I would suggest there is neither foundation nor is this document admissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: My question was purely technical, to see whether this was a -- just forgotten by the OTP but now it becomes something else, Mr. Demirdjian.

utterances.speaker: MR. DEMIRDJIAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'm not going to press on the matter. The witness gave his answers about the information he had at the time. He did say he had not seen the document at the time. We're satisfied with the answers on the record. So I'll withdraw my application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Demirdjian. Seems sensible. If there's nothing else, court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 2nd day of July, 2013, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.34 p.m.,
